title: Oops
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona's talk emphasizes the importance of taking responsibility for our actions and cultivating gratitude, particularly when we make mistakes. By acknowledging our flaws and using them as opportunities for growth, we can learn to recognize harm and take steps to prevent it in the future. This involves being honest with ourselves about our mistakes, rather than trying to hide or excuse them, and finding ways to grow and improve from them.

sentences.text: Oh, good idea.
The title of this talk is "Oops."
When I was in high school, there was a job fair.
We gave our résumés ahead of time to some of the companies on the list, and then went to talk to them at the job fair.
I went to the table of Shady Oaks Camp, and they asked me, "Why do you want to work at Shady Oaks Camp?"
I said, "Well, it sounds like it's in alignment with what I want to do, working with nature, a place to be away and have hiking trails and stuff."
The recruiter said, "Well, we do have a lot of trails.
But they're mostly covered in asphalt."
I said, "Oh."
He said, "But your résumé looks good.
Did you work on this yourself?"
Because I had done it on a computer, and this was the late 80s, when most were typed.
I said, "Yeah, I had some computer experience."
He said, "So Shady Oaks Camp is a camp for children with cerebral palsy.
Most of them are in wheelchairs; they couldn't walk on a path without asphalt.
And we've had this adaptive hardware donated to us, so that people who can't use their hands to use a keyboard could interface with a computer.
But none of us know how to use it.
It's just sitting there in a corner.
And we think you're the right person to figure out how to use it and build a program around it."
I said, "Okay," and I took that on.
I became a counselor at Shady Oaks Camp for children with cerebral palsy, noting that many of those children had been going to the camp for over 40 years.
They were children in the sense of being the child of somebody, but not young people.
At the camp, I hung out with a group of people who had clean fun, stuff like having a beach party in the sandbox after everybody had gone to bed.
Then come August was the Perseid meteor showers, and we were talking about where we could go to see the meteor shower.
One of the staff members, named Chuck, said, "Oh, I know the perfect place, in Chicago Heights."
We thought, "Oh, Chicago Heights.
This is by Chicago.
That sounds like a place where it'd be away from city lights, someplace that's up and above and would have a good view of the sky."
So six of us piled into somebody's Civic hatchback and drove for an hour and a half.
We got lost a couple of times.
Chuck was actually special in that he had been one of the campers with cerebral palsy.
He got around in a wheelchair, but with his upper body strength he was able to be a full camp counselor.
He'd been directing us for an hour and a half or so, and finally he said, "Yeah, that's it.
Pull over here."
We looked around and said, "But Chuck, there's all two-story buildings and streetlights everywhere.
How are we going to see the meteor showers?"
And Chuck said, "Meteor showers?
I thought we were going for burritos."
That was one of a few interesting confusions with Chuck.
There were a couple of others.
Once he had us convinced that we needed to paint the ceiling in the basement because we didn't want people to think that the roof leaked, until we said, "Hey, wait a minute, this is in the basement."
And there was a time when one of the premises of his arguments was that trains go from east to west.
I thought, "Wait a minute, if that was the case, we'd end up with this big pile of trains on the west coast."
Come the end of the year, camp counselors had our own special end-of-the-year celebration after all the campers were gone.
Each of us was asked to say something about our experience over the summer.
I stood up and gave my top three quotes from Chuck: painting the ceiling in the basement, the trains only go from east to west, and "I thought we were going for burritos."

Just as I said that, I realized that many of the campers not only had physical difficulties caused by the prebirth brain abnormality that is cerebral palsy, but many of them also had mental challenges.
It is likely that these were related to challenges that Chuck had, which was pretty much an invisible disability most of the time.
And here I was pointing that out, mocking that, in front of all of his friends.
And that's not something you can unsay.
Now, I once interviewed a man who had accidentally shot and killed his six-year-old daughter.
This doesn't rise to the level of something you can't undo like that.
But it's weighed heavily on me for 30 years now.
Consider an action that you regret.
There's a Zen story involving Fookai Hongko, a Zen master who lived 1779 to 1847.
The story isn't actually about him.
You've probably heard it.
It's actually about his cook, who was late getting the meal together one day and a bit rushed, and put together a vegetable soup that all the students thought was one of the best they'd ever had.
Until Master Fookai picked up with his chopsticks, out of the soup, a snakehead, and lifted it up.
A snakehead that probably accidentally got cut off as the cook was hurrying to cut the vegetables.
And he said, "Tanzo, cook."
The cook came up and bowed and said, "Oh, thank you, master," and took the snakehead and ate it.
This story is frequently taught with two points.
One, which I had always perceived to be the point, is taking responsibility for our actions, fully taking responsibility: "This is mine, I own it."
It's also part of, as Norman, I believe, tells a story in his book on the Lojong teachings, swallowing the blame, in the context of just letting there not be any, not worrying about the blame.
Maybe he wasn't the one who chopped up the vegetables.
Maybe it was somebody else, but he doesn't say, "Ah, geez, that assistant cook."

Lately I've been appreciating a new interpretation, for me, of that story, which is that maybe the cook genuinely felt gratitude and said, "Oh, thank you, master," with true gratitude for recognizing our mistakes.

For me, that has a big bearing on the story that I told to start with: if I hadn't had that horrible standing up and acting like a fourth grader in front of my friends, and Chuck's friends, how much more similar harm would I have done in the years since then?
So I'm truly grateful to have had that lesson.
That's part of the background to an important aspect of many of the ceremonies we do, where we start with confession.
Myself, as many of you have, we found in the Sangha, come from a Catholic background, and confession comes with some baggage.
Yet there is importance and beauty in it.
Just for one example, I'm going to jump to Chris's buddy Shantideva, for whom chapter two is about confession.

One thing that's interesting about his chapter, which mirrors much of our ceremonies, is that in the chapter on confession, he spends the first 27 verses making offerings, asking for support, asking for support from powers beyond ourselves, which we can think of as Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, as beings, or also the archetypes that they represent to us, that we need that help from humanity.
And just to read you a few of the chapters after all the offerings, then he states, there's some really heavy language in there, which Shantideva is wont to use on occasion.
And isn't it very interesting, that last line of who he is declaring to, who he is confessing to: the teachers, right, with the approach that recognizing the mistakes is an opportunity to learn.
And back to that, an opportunity for gratitude.
There's a footnote in here on that Catholic baggage that we carry.
The translator has a footnote saying, you might object to terms like sin, but without the context of the fall from the divine, the actual meaning of the word, a grave transgression, fits.
And he's listing that.
In [unclear: "Pema children's"] book on this, she highlights the importance of it as preparing the ground, right, that we're here to do something here in our practice.
And that this activity of recognizing our mistakes is preparing the ground.
The intention is not to focus on how messed up we are, but to let go of thoughts about "oops," and see new opportunities for us to refine our behaviors going into the future.
A good friend of mine in college wrote a book about his life, having run away from home at 16 years old and living on the streets for three years.
He talks about how he prostituted himself to get money to get by, and that when he did come across money, he didn't use it wisely.
It was easy come, easy go.
And the damage that it did to him, the prostituting, which started out by meeting basically a pedophile who befriended him on a bus, and it was money.
What really struck me was that when he did get money, he then went and hired a female prostitute and had sex with her.
That really got me thinking, and I appreciated his ability to talk about and share that, to sort of understand how it is that we go about making our mistakes.
When discussing it, we came up with a number of different types of error of action that causes harm to others.
One is not recognizing that our action is causing harm.
An example of that might be eating meat without knowing about how the animals were raised or caused harm.
The second type is recognizing an action causes harm but not perceiving that we're doing it.
These are just some categories we thought of to be able to think about it, right?
There's nothing solid or definite here.
But within that, there are sometimes times when we might say we should have known, like my experience with Chuck, where I'm mocking him.
I recognize at the time the harm that I was causing, but I probably should have.
Or there might be times when we identify something as causing harm but there's no way we could have known.
Another way is recognizing harm that we're doing and honestly trying not to do it, but not being able to control our actions.
That's where Evan felt that his hiring of the prostitute came in: he just went back to what he was familiar with.
Addictions probably fit into that category.
We recognize the harm, and yet we fail to stop doing it.
Another category would be recognizing that we're causing harm, but deciding to go ahead and do it.
Making a conscious decision, "I'm going to do this even though I recognize it."
A small example is the way we use energy, some of the trips we make, some of the fuel we use, or owning stock in a chemical company, for example.
And again, this is all way more black and white than reality, right?
There's the difficulty of judging whether we're doing more harm than good with something.
The fifth way that we're thinking about it is performing the action out of a desire to cause harm, which runs everywhere from using caustic words to hurt somebody all the way to violence.
So now, for context, right, there are some very serious life mistakes we're talking about there.
And then we have our [unclear: "Saga Petri dish"], and particularly an example being doing the bells of the chanting and how much we get upset by the mistakes we make when doing that.
I've told this story before.
When I was doing [unclear: "male bells"] when Norman was Doshi, usually after the priest makes the offering, if there's a bell, it means that we're all going to do bowing now.
If there's a bell before they get back to the mat, right, that means we're all going to get out of our mats and start bowing.
And so there was a time we weren't supposed to be doing bowing.
He was supposed to be going on to Jundo.
But I made a mistake and I hit the bell as he did that bow to the altar.
He followed right along and got out his bowing [unclear: "that"].
And I'm forgetting the word for it, but the [unclear: "protect for protecting your case"], and ended his bows.

And again, similar to the story with Chuck, I am so grateful for that mistake, because it helped me understand how much of a two-way communication it is between the bell ringer and the priest who's doing the service.
So in a world of mistakes that cause tremendous suffering, what's the worst that happens when we make a mistake doing the bells or doing the chanting?
Those are mistakes that are a lot easier to have gratitude for.
And those are the thoughts that I had for tonight.
I suspect that it has brought up some other thoughts that you might have about causing harm and making mistakes and gratitude for them.
So what do you say, [unclear: "narrator"]?
Can we go to inviting other people to speak?
